content: The implementation of alcohol taxation and pricing policies requires a robust administrative framework to establish and collect taxes effectively. This framework must include a comprehensive understanding of the alcohol market within the jurisdiction where the policies are to be applied. Taxes on alcoholic beverages can be collected at various points, such as when the products are imported, released for distribution from domestic production facilities or tax-free storage, or sold to consumers through retail establishments. Typically, alcohol excise duties are collected by customs and excise officers from importers and producers when the products enter the wholesale or retail market. To facilitate tax collection, it is necessary to register or license all alcohol importers, producers, and manufacturing facilities. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends regulatory mechanisms for alcohol production, importation, and wholesaling to streamline taxation procedures. These regulations can also serve health and safety purposes. Effective alcohol taxation as a public health strategy depends on pre-existing customs and excise systems, which should already be in place to ensure smooth implementation. Tax collection from importers and local producers involves fewer points of enforcement compared to sales taxes, making it more manageable. Accurate planning of alcohol taxation requires knowledge of total alcohol consumption, including both recorded and unrecorded sales, as well as consumption patterns across different beverage categories such as beer, wine, spirits, and other locally significant products. Studies on price elasticity and drinking habits can provide valuable insights for estimating the impact of new tax decisions. Effective tax administration demands high compliance from taxpayers and low administrative costs relative to revenue collected. This requires technical capacity within the administrative agency and a well-designed tax system that is transparent, simple, and unified. A unified excise tax system, where all alcohol products are taxed at the same level, can generate revenue, reduce alcohol consumption and related harms, and prevent the initiation of drinking. Specific taxation methods may be more suitable for high-income countries with a high prevalence of drinkers, while mixed taxation methods or minimum pricing policies may be more appropriate for lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) with a high prevalence of lifetime abstainers. Governments should set clear goals for taxation and pricing policies, such as generating revenue, reducing alcohol consumption and harms, and preventing drinking initiation. They should also select the taxation method that best achieves these goals and determine the simplest possible tax rate system to minimize complexity. Tax administration must include strategies to enhance compliance and reduce opportunities for tax avoidance and evasion. Effective administration relies on cooperation between taxpayers and tax authorities, with enforcement actions such as audits and measures to combat illicit activities. Physical controls and tax stamps are commonly used to ensure compliance. Enhanced tax stamps, such as banderoles, and digital tax stamps provide advanced tracking and tracing systems to reduce tax evasion. These systems require manufacturers to comply with monitoring processes, which electronically transmit production data to the finance ministry for real-time tracking and enforcement. Tax avoidance and evasion pose significant challenges to maintaining a stable tax revenue base, particularly after tax increases. Tax avoidance involves legal activities to reduce tax payments, such as purchasing goods from lower-tax jurisdictions, while tax evasion involves illegal activities to avoid taxes. Producers may engage in tax avoidance by altering product characteristics or pricing strategies to minimize tax burdens. For example, manipulating alcohol concentration or packaging can reduce the tax liability on certain products. The substitution effect is another critical consideration in alcohol taxation. Studies show that beer has lower price elasticity compared to wine or spirits, likely because it is a common beverage consumed daily in many countries. In contrast, wine, which was once considered a luxury item in some regions, now exhibits higher price elasticity, indicating that it is viewed as a necessity by some consumers. Governments must account for potential substitution effects when implementing differential tax rate policies, as changes in the price of one type of alcohol may lead to increased consumption of other substances, including illicit drugs or homemade spirits, depending on cultural and social contexts. Affordability is a key factor in determining the effectiveness of alcohol taxation. In many countries, alcohol has become more affordable over time due to declining prices and inflation eroding the impact of excise duties. To address this, governments should have legislation that allows for regular adjustments of tax rates to account for inflation. Changes in income levels within a country can also affect alcohol affordability and consumption. Increases in alcohol prices alone may not be sufficient to reduce consumption if other factors influencing demand counteract the price effect. This is particularly relevant in LMICs, where affordability may have a greater impact on consumption patterns. Finally, the Nordic alcohol tax study highlights the complexities of taxation policies. For example, Denmark and Finland reduced excise duty rates to combat increases in travelers’ alcohol imports after the abolition of duty-free quotas. While Denmark did not experience significant changes in alcohol consumption or related harms, Finland saw an increase in both consumption and associated harms. This underscores the importance of considering local contexts and potential unintended consequences when designing and implementing alcohol taxation and pricing policies.
